plan.analysis: The seed uniform f gives R=2/3 (triangle autoconvolution). To beat it, the autoconvolution must be flatter than a triangle: more mass away from its central peak. I bet on two concrete shape families plus one free-form search. The U-shaped family (higher at the ends) and the central-gap family both test whether removing central mass flattens f*f enough to raise the L2/Linf ratio. Free-form hill climbing on heights is a catch-all in case the optimum is not in these simple families. All start from the best constant construction and use the full 30 s.

plan.analysis: p0002 reached 0.833 at N=50 with coordinate-wise accept-only refinement; p0006 (N=300) got 0.822 and p0003 (N=800) 0.803 — higher N alone fails, but p0002 was never refined *after* upsampling a good shape (its upsample stage was applied to the constant seed, which never helped). So the obvious untapped move is: keep the strong N=50 shape, then upsample and refine at successively finer N. Second, all searches so far are derivative-free coordinate hill climbs; a smooth-max (p-norm) reformulation of R with scipy L-BFGS-B is a genuinely different search that could reach a finer optimum. Third, single-coordinate moves ignore coupling between neighbours, so pairwise coordinate refinement is a cheap way to escape p0002's local optimum at N=50.

experiments.hypothesis: p0002's 0.833 shape is a good coarse approximation of the continuous optimum; refining it at N=50, then upsampling that shape and refining at N~150 and N~400 will beat 0.833 because the earlier high-N failures started from the constant seed, not from a good shape.
experiments.change: construct(budget,start): take h=start (upsample/pad to N=50 if needed) and best=exact score. Run stage loop over n in [50,150,400] (skip interpolation if n==len(h); else np.interp to n). For each stage with its own deadline (0,~8,~20,~36 s of the 0.9*budget): run coordinate descent over random permutations of all indices; for each index i try factors {1.5,1.25,1.1,1.05,0.95,0.9,0.8,0.67} (multiplicative, h[i]>0 enforced), accept the first/best improving one; additionally each pass do 5 block moves (random contiguous block length 2-6 scaled by {1.1,0.9}) and one smooth perturbation (random low-frequency cosine, amplitude ~0.005) with accept-if-improve. Keep the globally best array and return it (the coarse solution is a fallback if an upsample stage does not improve). Time-guard with time.process_time and leave ~2 s margin.
experiments.prediction: Score rises above 0.840, and the final returned N is >50, confirming that resolution on top of a good shape helps.
experiments.if_gain: Push the ladder further (N=800, 1600) from the new best next generation, and inspect whether the shape converges.
experiments.if_not: Conclude N=50 is essentially saturated and that increasing N from a good shape does not pay under 40 s; then go all-in on the smooth gradient approach and on larger-N annealing.

experiments.hypothesis: R's only non-smoothness is ||f*f||_inf = max L_j. Replacing it with an L_p norm (p raised progressively) gives a smooth objective whose gradient optimizes all heights jointly — something no experiment has done — and should reach a better optimum near p0002's.
experiments.change: construct(budget,start): h0 = start (keep its N, e.g. 50, and also try an interpolated N=100 copy). Define L=np.convolve(h,h); S1=sum(h)**2; S2=sum((L_j^2+L_j L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2)/3); obj(h,p) = -(log(S2) - log(S1) - (1/p)*log(sum(L**p + 1e-300))), computing via scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B', bounds=[(1e-8,None)]*n, options with small maxiter). Continuation p in [8,16,32,64,128], warm-starting each stage from the previous, with a hard process_time deadline per stage (rescale h to unit sum between stages). After each stage evaluate the EXACT score and keep the best array; if L-BFGS-B returns nothing better than start within its share of time, spend the remaining time on the p0002-style coordinate descent so the budget is never wasted. Return the best exact-score array. Leave ~2 s margin.
experiments.prediction: L-BFGS-B with p-continuation finds a score >0.840 at the starting N, or at least shows steady per-stage improvement; if it stalls we learn the landscape near p0002 is not smoothly improvable.
experiments.if_gain: Combine both: use L-BFGS-B polish as the final stage of the multiscale ladder (large N) next generation, and raise p further.
experiments.if_not: Report it as smooth-optimization failure on this state; rely on stochastic multiscale and pairwise moves, and investigate whether max is attained at many nearly-equal knots (making the p-norm ill-conditioned).

experiments.if_not: Treat p0002 as locally tight at N=50 and allocate everything to resolution ladders and gradient methods.

plan.analysis: Two strong, complementary results exist: p0009's pairwise moves lifted the N=50 shape from 0.833 to 0.854 (F6), and p0011's resolution ladder reached 0.850 at N=400 using only single-coordinate descent (F5). They have never been combined: pairwise moves on an upsampled good shape is the most obvious untapped gain. Second, all moves so far are random; the score's only non-smoothness is the max knot, and ~38% of knots sit within 5% of it, so moves targeted at the knots nearest the maximum should raise R far more efficiently than blind pairs. Third, p0009's restarts perturb only 1%; a wider basin-hopping test tells us whether 0.854 is a local basin or near the true optimum at N=50. I bet on the combination first, targeting second, escape third.

experiments.hypothesis: p0009 showed pairwise coupling is what unlocked 0.833->0.854 at N=50, and p0011 showed a good shape refined at N=400 gives 0.850 with single-coordinate moves only. Applying p0009's pairwise moves after each upsample stage will beat both: the coarse shape gets its neighbour coupling fixed, then fine resolution adds the remaining plateau flatness.
experiments.change: Keep p0011's construct skeleton and _pad_to, but replace _coord_descent with p0009-style pairwise refinement: pick random i and offset d in {-3..3}\{0}, wrap j=(i+d)%n, try the 5x5 factor grid {0.8,0.9,1.0,1.1,1.25} on (h[i],h[j]) with exact score, accept the best improving pair, then ~8 random local refinements (factors 1+N(0,0.03)) around it; repeat until the stage deadline. Stage schedule over the whole budget: N=50 for 0-25%, upsample by np.interp to N=150 for 25-55%, upsample to N=400 for the rest; keep and return the globally best array across stages (all stages scored with the exact R, comparable across N). Time-guard with process_time and leave a 2 s margin.

experiments.if_not: Conclude fine resolution does not pay beyond N=50 under pairwise moves and put all budget into N=50 pairwise/max-targeted search.

plan.analysis: p0017 (0.857288) shows max-targeted moves are the strongest N=50 search so far (+0.0034), but they have never been combined with a resolution ladder (p0019 only did blind pairs and stalled at 0.855), and p0014 independently reached 0.8567 via smooth L_p gradient polish — a genuinely different global step never applied to p0017's shape. The N=50 basin appears narrow (F10: 6% hops fail), so the best leverage is (a) extending max-targeted moves to finer grids, (b) making the targeting systematic rather than random (descend on every pair forming the argmax knot, not one random split), and (c) polishing p0017's shape globally with the smooth-max gradient method. Bet: systematic targeting is cheapest and most likely to gain; ladder and polish are the two orthogonal escapes from the narrow basin.

experiments.hypothesis: Max-targeted moves lowered the knot count near max at N=50 (F8), but p0019's ladder used only blind pair moves and stalled at 0.855. Applying p0017's max-targeted inner loop after each upsample should let fine resolution add plateau flatness on top of the better-targeted coarse shape.

plan.analysis: Gains have shrunk to +0.0007 per generation. p0022's max-targeted ladder (F11) still gains at every rung, but its inner loop recomputes a full O(N^2) convolution for every candidate (25+ evaluations per move), so the fine grids are badly iteration-starved. The biggest untapped lever is therefore speed: an exact O(N) rank-2 update of the autoconvolution makes ~100x more moves affordable at N=400-800. Second, the binding constraint is the top of the L array (40% of knots within 5% of max); a top-m flatness surrogate attacks that directly instead of accepting only exact-R improvements. Third, the 5x5 factor grid is a coarse move primitive — a continuous 1-D optimization of a single height tests whether the fine grid, not the method, is what saturates.

experiments.hypothesis: p0022's stages still improved at N=400 (16.85% -> fewer knots within 0.1% of max) but each accepted move costs ~25 full np.convolve evaluations; a change of two heights is a rank-2 update of L, computable exactly in O(N). experiments.change: Keep p0022's construct skeleton and staged structure. On acceptance update h and keep newL; every 100 accepted moves resync L = np.convolve(h,h) and recompute to control drift. Raise the Gaussian local-refinement loop from 8 to 20 steps. plan.analysis: Every gain since gen 5 came from the fast incremental ladder (F15/F18/F21) and, once, from block moves (F22) or basin hops (F19); single-height sweeps and surrogates are dead. The per-doubling return of the ladder is still ~+3e-5 (800→2400→4800), so discretization is not yet saturated at N=5000 — but the return halves each rung, so the total remaining resolution loss is probably ~2e-5. Two axes are underexplored at the new frontier: (a) block/bump moves, which reshape the 20%-of-knots near-max plateau that 2-of-5000 pair moves cannot, and (b) the basin structure itself: every shape found so far has 0% zero heights and ratio ~3.2, so a gapped/sparse profile has never been tested since the crude parametric gen-1 runs. I bet on one more resolution rung, block moves at the fine frontier, and one open search over gapped shapes compared head-to-head with the best at the same N.
